Storage Auction Max Bid Calculator

How Long Do You Have to Clean Out a Storage Unit You Won?

The removal window starts the moment the hammer falls, not when you're ready for it. Miss it and the refundable cleanout deposit is what's at risk — not the bid itself.

The window is set by the facility, not by a single nationwide rule

Most operators require the unit emptied within 24 to 72 hours of winning, but the exact number is a term of that specific auction listing, not a fixed law you can assume from one facility to the next. An in-person lockout auction commonly posts a same-day or next-day deadline; some online platforms give a few days. The window belongs to the unit you're bidding on, so read its own removal terms before you bid rather than carrying over what a different facility, or a forum post, said last time.

What is close to universal is the mechanism: a refundable cleanout deposit, commonly in the same rough range as a cheap dump run, held against two things — clearing the unit inside the window, and leaving it broom-clean when you do. Meet both and it comes back. Miss either and some or all of it is kept, sometimes alongside losing the right to bid at that facility again.

Crew size changes wall-clock time, not total labor

The window measures wall-clock hours, not effort, and those are not the same number. Total labor is fixed by how much is actually in the unit; wall-clock time is that total divided across however many people are hauling at once.

Total cleanout laborSoloCrew of 2Crew of 3
6 person-hours6.0 hrs3.0 hrs2.0 hrs
10 person-hours10.0 hrs5.0 hrs3.3 hrs
16 person-hours16.0 hrs8.0 hrs5.3 hrs

A 10-person-hour unit sized around a solo cleanout looks comfortably inside a 48-hour window on paper, and still misses it if the second person you were counting on has to cancel — the plan had no slack, only a smaller number divided by a crew that turned out to be one. Pricing the labor line against the crew size you can actually count on, not the one you hope shows up, is what keeps the deposit safe rather than at risk.

What actually eats the clock on cleanout day

  • The first sort-and-bag pass. Nothing else starts until trash, sellable items, and dump-only items are split, and this is the step people underestimate because it looks like it should be fast.
  • Dump runs, not just driving. Transfer stations queue, weigh, and charge on the spot — budget the wait, not just the drive time, and bring a way to pay there rather than expecting an invoice later.
  • Re-securing the unit. The facility's lock comes off the moment you win and stays off until you put your own on, so the unit isn't secured again on your behalf in between.
  • A dolly for anything more than a few steps from the truck. Furniture and boxed goods move at a fraction of the speed by hand that they do on wheels, and that gap compounds over a full unit.

None of this shows up in a headline bid number. All of it either costs money directly (dump fees, a truck) or costs wall-clock time against a deposit that's only refundable if the unit is empty and clean before the window closes. This calculator's cleanout fields turn total labor hours and crew size into that wall-clock figure and flags it the moment it exceeds the window you enter, so the deposit risk is a number you see before you bid rather than a surprise the next morning.

Common questions

How long do storage facilities typically give you to clean out a unit after you win?

Commonly 24 to 72 hours, set by the facility's own auction terms rather than by a uniform law — some in-person auctioneers post a same-day or next-day deadline, while some online platforms allow a few days. Read the specific listing's removal terms before you bid; the window you assume from a different facility or a forum post is not a fact about the unit in front of you.

What does the cleanout deposit actually protect the facility against?

Two things: a unit left occupied past the window, which blocks the facility from renting it out again, and a unit left in bad condition, which costs the facility labor to finish clearing. The deposit is refundable when you clear it out on time and leave it broom-clean; miss either condition and some or all of it is kept. It is a bond against your own performance, not a fee you're paying for the privilege of bidding.

Does a bigger crew actually buy you more time?

It buys you less wall-clock time for the same total labor, which is the thing the window actually measures. Ten person-hours of sorting and hauling is a full workday solo, about five hours with a second person, or a bit over three with a crew of three — the facility's clock does not care how many people are working, only when the unit is empty. A bid sized around solo-hours can look safely inside a 48-hour window on paper and still miss it if the helper you were counting on cancels.

What is worth bringing on cleanout day that people forget?

A padlock of your own, since the facility's lock comes off the moment you win and the unit is not secured again until you close it back up. Contractor bags and boxes for the fast sort-and-bag pass that has to happen before anything else, a dolly if the unit is more than a few steps from the truck, and cash or a card for the dump fee at the transfer station, which most operators want on the spot rather than billed later. None of that shows up in a headline bid number, and all of it either costs money or costs time against the window.

FOR STORAGE AUCTION BUYERS

The 20%-of-value rule can bid you past your own break-even before you've paid for a dump run.

A lien-auction unit is sold sight-mostly-unseen, and every forum repeats the same rule: don't bid more than 20-30% of what it's worth. That rule skips the buyer's premium charged on top of your bid, prices "worth" at retail instead of realistic resale recovery, and has no room at all for dump, labor, transport and holding cost. This free calculator prices the real cost stack and reports what it actually supports. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Bought jewelry or scrap in the unit? The scrap gold buy price calculator works out what a lot of gold is worth after the refiner's cut and fees.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Your value estimate, bid, and cost numbers are never uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is saved when you close the tab. Copy shareable link is the one way these figures leave this device, and only because you choose to send them: they ride in the page's URL fragment, which a browser never puts in a request line or a Referer header. We count only anonymous local feature events (bid-calculated, overbid-warning-shown, link_copied) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no values, bids, or unit details are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Is the winning bid what I actually pay?

No. Lien-auction platforms and most in-person auctioneers charge a buyer's premium on top of your hammer bid, commonly 10-15%. If you bid $400 with a 12% premium, your actual purchase price is $448, not $400. This calculator applies the premium to every figure it reports, so the ceiling it gives you is a hammer bid, and the total-outlay figure next to your planned bid already includes the premium.

Why isn't the max bid just a percentage of what the contents are worth?

Because a flat percentage skips two real cuts and ignores a real cost stack. What the contents would fetch new or with time to negotiate is not what a stranger's used goods net on a resale deadline — that is the recovery rate. What they do net is then cut again by resale channel and payment fees. And the cash cost of dump runs, a truck, cleanout labor and holding inventory while you sell it does not scale with the unit's value at all, so a percentage rule has no room for it — which is exactly backwards on a small or hard-to-sell unit, the outcome you cannot rule out sight-unseen.

What is the difference between the break-even bid and the max bid at my target margin?

The break-even bid is the hammer price at which this deal nets exactly $0 profit — the absolute ceiling past which every extra dollar is a loss. The max bid at your target margin is lower: it is the bid that leaves your required profit margin on the table, not just avoids a loss. Bidding between the two can still be a real deal, just a thinner one than your target; bidding past the break-even bid is a loss no matter how the resale goes.

What happens if I don't clean out the unit in time?

Facilities set a removal window — commonly 24 to 72 hours — and most require a refundable cleanout deposit that you forfeit if you miss it or leave the unit in bad condition, sometimes alongside being barred from future auctions there. This calculator divides your total cleanout labor hours by your crew size to get the wall-clock hours the job actually takes, and flags it when that exceeds the facility's window, so the deposit risk is a number you see before you bid, not a surprise the next morning.

Does anything about my bid or my numbers get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only, there is no account, and nothing you type is uploaded. Nothing leaves this device unless you choose to send it: the Copy shareable link button puts the figures on the form into the page's URL fragment, which a browser never sends to a server or into a Referer header, so it reaches only the person you hand the link to. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button below.

vs-bidding-a-flat-percentage.html.text:
← Storage Auction Max Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. bidding a flat percentage of value

Every storage-auction forum repeats some version of the same rule: don't bid more than 20-30% of what the unit is worth. That rule prices "worth" at retail instead of realistic resale recovery, skips the buyer's premium charged on top of your bid, and has no room at all for the cash cost of cleanout. This page shows exactly where it goes wrong, with the calculator's own worked example.

Where the percentage rule breaks down

A flat percentage-of-value rule is popular because it needs almost nothing to apply: eyeball the contents, multiply by a number you already remember, bid. That is also exactly why it misses three real costs that do not scale the same way the eyeballed value does.

The winning bid is not the purchase price. Lien-auction platforms and most in-person auctioneers charge a buyer's premium on top of the hammer price, commonly 10-15%. A bidder applying a percentage rule to their walk-away number is quietly bidding past it every time the premium is not already backed out.

"What it's worth" and "what it nets you" are different numbers, twice over. A percentage rule is usually applied to an eyeballed retail value. Liquidating a stranger's unit on a resale deadline realizes a fraction of that as used goods with no provenance, and whatever it does fetch is cut again by the resale channel's own fees.

Cleanout has its own cash cost, and it does not scale with the contents' value. Dump loads, a truck, labor hours, and months of holding cost to resell through are roughly the same size whether the unit holds antiques or a sofa nobody wants -- and a percentage-of-value rule has no room for a fixed cost stack at all, which is exactly backwards on a small or hard-to-sell unit, the outcome you cannot rule out sight-unseen.

On the default worked exampleWhat it says to bid
Flat 20%-of-value rule ($4,000 estimated retail)$800 — past the unit's own break-even, a guaranteed loss before cleanout starts
This calculator's break-even bid (0% margin, the absolute ceiling)$482.14
This calculator's bid at a 40% target margin$57.14
QuestionWhere to answer it
What's 20-30% of what I think this unit is worth?Either one — that arithmetic is one multiplication.
Does that percentage already account for the buyer's premium on top of my bid?This calculator — the premium is applied to every figure it reports, including the max-bid ceiling.
Does "worth" mean retail, or what a stranger's used goods actually net on a resale deadline?This calculator — a separate recovery-rate and resale-fee input, not one blended guess.
Does the rule account for dump loads, labor, transport, and holding cost?This calculator — the full cash cost stack, priced against net resale revenue before a bid is ever suggested.
Does my planned bid clear break-even, or just look thin?This calculator — break-even and target-margin are reported as two separate numbers, not one blended guess.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No, on either — but a percentage rule needs no tool at all, and gives you no way to check it against the real cost stack.

A rule of thumb is a reasonable starting guess when you have thirty seconds at a lockout and no calculator. This page is not an argument against having a fast number in your head — it is that the fast number and the real math can disagree by an order of magnitude, and only the real math tells you when they have.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

What does the flat percentage-of-value rule actually get wrong?

Three things. The winning bid is not the purchase price — lien-auction platforms and most in-person auctioneers charge a buyer's premium on top of the hammer bid, commonly 10-15%, and a percentage rule applied to the hammer number quietly bids past it every time. Retail value and realistic net resale value are different numbers, twice over: a flat percentage is usually applied to an eyeballed retail value, but liquidating a stranger's unit on a deadline realizes only a fraction of that as used goods with no provenance, and whatever it does fetch is cut again by the resale channel's own fees. And cleanout has its own cash cost — dump loads, a truck, labor hours, and holding cost — that does not scale with the contents' value at all, which a percentage-of-value rule has no room for.

How far off can a flat 20%-of-value bid actually be?

On this calculator's own default worked example — a $4,000 estimated retail value, 35% realistic recovery, 15% blended resale fees, and a $650 cleanout cost stack — the flat 20%-of-value rule says bid up to $800. The real math supports a $57.14 hammer bid at a 40% target margin, and the unit's own break-even bid (0% margin, the absolute ceiling) is $482.14. An $800 bid is not just thinner than target, it is a guaranteed loss before cleanout even starts.

Does a percentage rule ever get close to the right number?

It can, on a unit whose recovery rate and cleanout cost happen to sit near whatever assumptions produced the rule of thumb in the first place — but nothing about the rule tells you when that is true, because it has no recovery rate, no resale fee, and no cost stack built into it at all. This calculator does not replace the percentage rule with a different flat number; it prices your break-even and target-margin bid from the actual inputs for the unit in front of you, and reports the naive rule's own bid alongside them so you can see directly whether it over- or under-shoots.

Is this page telling me never to use a rule of thumb?

No — a rule of thumb is a reasonable starting guess when you have thirty seconds at a lockout and no calculator. The point is narrower: know which number you're using. A percentage rule is a guess at what the real math would say; this calculator is the real math, run on the estimate you can make from the doorway. If the two agree, the rule happened to be right this time. If they don't, this page's break-even and target-margin figures are the ones your money is actually exposed to.

vs-storagetreasures.html.text:
← Storage Auction Max Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. StorageTreasures

Two different jobs: StorageTreasures is where facilities list lien-sale units and run the auction itself. This page is a free, private worksheet for the question that comes before you bid anywhere — what does the real cost stack say your bid should be.

What each tool is for

StorageTreasures is an online marketplace where self-storage facilities across the United States list units that have gone to lien sale and run public auctions for the contents, including online and live-online formats a remote bidder can join without visiting the facility. Bidding is done through a registered account, and, as on other lien-auction platforms, the winning bid is not the final price — a buyer's premium is charged on top of the hammer price. StorageTreasures' own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific fee percentages, deposit terms, or plan details, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure or percentage for it appears on this page. What StorageTreasures does not do is tell a bidder what to bid: it lists the unit, runs the clock, and takes the winning number.

This calculator does none of what StorageTreasures does. It does not list units, run an auction, or take a bid. It takes the numbers a bidder already has standing in front of a unit — an estimated retail value, a realistic resale recovery rate, blended resale channel fees, the buyer's premium, and the full cleanout cost stack (dump loads, transport, labor, and holding cost while reselling) — and turns them into the hammer bid that leaves a target profit margin, the break-even bid past which every extra dollar is a guaranteed loss, and the gap against the flat percent-of-value rule most auction forums repeat. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or StorageTreasures?

They do different jobs, and a bidder normally uses both. StorageTreasures is an online marketplace where self-storage facilities list units that have gone to lien sale and run the auctions themselves, in person or online, for the public to bid on; bidding on it is done through a registered account. StorageTreasures' own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific fee percentages, deposit terms, or plan details, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure or percentage for it appears on this page. This calculator does a different, narrower thing: given a unit's estimated retail value, a realistic resale recovery rate, resale channel fees, the buyer's premium, and the full cleanout cost stack, it works out the hammer bid your target margin supports, the break-even bid past which every dollar is a loss, and whether the flat percent-of-value rule most forums repeat over- or under-shoots that math. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A bidder finds and bids on units through StorageTreasures or a comparable auction platform; this calculator is the private worksheet for deciding what to bid before doing either.
